stories.headline: S&P 500 and Dow fall into correction as the sell-off in AI stocks deepens
stories.summary: The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday, and both it and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, meaning at least 10% below their record highs. The Nasdaq composite gave up its gain for 2026 and, according to MarketWatch, had its worst week since 2020. Chipmakers led the declines, and shares of Anthropic slid on their second day of trading after the largest IPO on record.
stories.why_it_matters: Most retirement accounts and index funds hold large positions in the technology companies leading this decline, so a correction shows up directly in 401(k) and savings balances. Outlets across the spectrum covered the drop.
stories.background: A handful of very large technology companies tied to artificial intelligence drove most of the stock market's gains this year, and because of their size they weigh heavily on the main indexes. Since early November investors have been selling those shares amid questions about whether the heavy spending on AI chips and data centers will pay off. A correction is the common term for a drop of 10% or more from a recent high. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after a record-size IPO, and some investors had hoped a strong debut would steady AI stocks. Interest rates are also a factor: Federal Reserve officials have been signaling further rate increases to fight inflation.

facts.text: The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday and the Nasdaq composite turned negative for the year, the Associated Press reported.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average both closed in correction territory, down 10% from their records.
Chipmakers led Friday's decline in U.S. stocks, according to Bloomberg.
The Nasdaq composite had its worst week since 2020, and all 11 S&P 500 sectors lost more than 1% for the week for the first time since April 2025, MarketWatch reported.
Anthropic's shares slid on Friday, their second day of trading, but stayed above the IPO price; the Wall Street Journal reported they came within 5 cents of it at one point.
The Wall Street Journal put the week's loss in AI-related stock value at about $4 trillion.
Stock markets in Asia and Europe also fell on Friday, with UK shares pulled down by banks and miners.
Reuters reported that U.S. investors moved money into value stocks during the technology sell-off.
Bitcoin fell to its lowest level in two years, Reuters reported.
On the prediction market Kalshi, the odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000, once above 70%, fell to very low levels, CNBC reported.

stories.headline: Fed's Cook says rate increases are needed as Trump and Bessent press for easier policy
stories.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said on Friday that interest rate increases are needed to bring down high inflation, Reuters reported. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued for a smaller increase, citing an energy price shock, and President Trump again said the Fed should lower rates. The Hill reported that Fed officials are likely to raise borrowing costs at their next meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: The Fed's rate decisions feed through to mortgage, car loan and credit card rates, and the prospect of higher rates is one of the pressures on stock prices.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve sets a short-term interest rate that influences borrowing costs across the economy; it raises the rate to slow inflation and lowers it to support growth and jobs. Inflation has been rising, with consumer prices up 3.7% from a year earlier in the latest reading in the ingest's market table, well above the Fed's 2% goal. Oil prices rose sharply because of the war involving Iran, and the administration argues that this kind of supply shock should not be met with rate increases. The Fed is designed to set rates independently of the White House, and President Trump has repeatedly pressed it to cut. Lisa Cook is one of the Fed's governors, who vote on rates.

facts.text: Fed Governor Lisa Cook said rate increases are needed to lower high inflation, Reuters reported.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued for a smaller Fed rate increase and cited the energy shock, Reuters reported.
President Trump on Friday repeated his view that the Fed should lower interest rates, while officials are likely to raise them at their upcoming meeting, The Hill reported.
The Chicago Fed president said inflation is headed the "wrong way", according to Fox Business.
A market strategist told Fox Business that inflation data due next week could affect the Fed's rate decisions.
On Nov. 13, Bessent said the Fed should not raise rates in response to an energy supply shock tied to the Iran war, Al Jazeera reported.

Bessent said the energy shock is a reason for the Fed to raise rates by less; Reuters earlier reported that he and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee were divided on the role of the energy shock in inflation.

stories.headline: California subpoenas Nvidia over China chip sales; Trump says Huang should apologize and return
stories.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia, asking whether its advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether the company misled investors and the public. On Friday President Trump said former chief executive Jensen Huang should apologize and go back to work at Nvidia and that he still backs Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said no further restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to China are needed.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is among the most widely held U.S. stocks, so legal and export-control risk at the company reaches ordinary investors, and the dispute bears on how strictly the U.S. limits advanced chip sales to China.
stories.background: Nvidia designs the chips used to train and run most advanced AI systems, and the U.S. restricts which of them may be sold to China. Jensen Huang, the company's co-founder and longtime chief executive, left the company this month amid a scandal; the Associated Press has reported allegations that he had an affair with a former executive of a chip buyer whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China, which Beijing denies. The Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, writes export-control rules, and Lutnick has faced questions about whether limits on Nvidia sales were delayed. An investigative subpoena is a demand for information and is not an accusation of wrongdoing.

facts.text: California's attorney general served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia to examine whether the company misled investors.
The California Department of Justice said it is asking whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public.
Bonta said the scandal "raises bright red flags", the Guardian reported.
Trump said Huang should apologize and return to Nvidia, and said he still backs Lutnick.
Bloomberg described Huang's return as chief executive as highly unlikely.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said no further restrictions are needed on Nvidia chip exports to China, the Associated Press reported.
A week earlier, on Nov. 13, Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for not restricting Nvidia chip exports to China, the Associated Press reported.
Lutnick is facing scrutiny over Nvidia chip exports to China, Fox Business reported.
Nvidia's stock fell on Friday, according to Fox Business.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO total rises to $93.5 billion as its shares slide toward the offer price
stories.summary: Anthropic's initial public offering grew to $93.5 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares, Reuters and CNBC reported. The stock fell on Friday, its second day of trading, and at one point was 5 cents above the $83 offer price, according to the Wall Street Journal. NPR reported that the debut also drew protests and questions from critics about the company's influence and its safety commitments.
stories.why_it_matters: It is the largest IPO on record, and brokerages such as Robinhood and Vanguard gave individual investors access to the shares, so their early swings affect ordinary buyers as well as funds.
stories.background: Anthropic is the AI company that makes the Claude models and is, with OpenAI, at the center of the AI industry. It priced its IPO at $83 a share and began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday; the Wall Street Journal called it the biggest IPO in history. A greenshoe, or overallotment, is an option that lets the banks running an IPO buy extra shares from the company at the offer price, which increases the amount raised. The company has said it puts safety ahead of commercial success, and critics question whether that will hold now that it answers to public shareholders. The debut came during a broad sell-off in AI stocks.

facts.text: The IPO total rose to $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised the overallotment option.
Anthropic sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares at $83 each, CNBC reported.
The base offering, before the option, was 980 million shares and raised about $81.3 billion.
The shares rose about 17% on Thursday, their first day of trading.
On Friday the stock fell and at one point was 5 cents above its IPO price, the Wall Street Journal reported; MarketWatch reported it stayed above the IPO price.
NPR reported that the first day of trading drew protests and criticism over whether the company can be a responsible steward of AI technology.
Axios reported that shareholders will watch whether Anthropic can become a business that does not need repeated capital infusions from investors and vendors.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI takes in $3.79 billion on its first day, Rockstar says
stories.summary: Rockstar Games said Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, which it called the biggest launch in entertainment history. The figure comes from the company and its parent, Take-Two Interactive, and is about five times what the previous game in the series made on its first day in 2013.
stories.why_it_matters: The launch is a measure of consumer spending going into the holiday season and a rare piece of good corporate news in a week of market losses.
stories.background: Grand Theft Auto is a video game series made by Rockstar Games, which is owned by the publicly traded Take-Two Interactive. The sixth main game arrived 13 years after Grand Theft Auto V, which made roughly $800 million on its first day. The first-day sales figure was announced by the publisher itself. Outlets on the left, center and right all covered the announcement, most of them carrying the Associated Press report.

facts.text: Rockstar Games reported a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales for Grand Theft Auto VI.
That is nearly five times the roughly $800 million Grand Theft Auto V made on its first day in 2013, the New York Post reported.
The game arrived after a 13-year gap in the series, and no film has made more than $3 billion at the box office, the New York Times reported.
Before the announcement, the research firm Sensor Tower had estimated about $1.84 billion in sales by release day.
